C004.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work self-reported productivity]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment comparing self-reported productivity of remote vs. in-office teams on collaborative tasks with real-time feedback loops — Directly tests the causal claim under the specified condition, controlling for task type and feedback frequency.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of survey studies on remote work and subjective productivity, specifically filtering for tasks requiring frequent collaboration — Synthesizes existing self-report data to assess consistency and effect size across populations, clarifying whether the condition moderates the relationship.

[PATH:theoretical] Cognitive load theory and attention residue models applied to remote collaboration contexts — Provides mechanistic explanation for why real-time feedback might be less effective remotely, generating testable predictions about self-reported productivity.

qualifier.condition: for tasks requiring frequent collaboration and real-time feedback

C005.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work self-reported productivity]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal surveys of self-reported productivity among remote workers in high-income countries during 2020-2021 (e.g., from Stanford's WFH Research project or OECD datasets) — Directly measures the claimed effect in the specified temporal and geographic scope, allowing comparison of self-reported productivity changes over time and across demographics.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published studies on remote work and self-reported productivity during the pandemic (e.g., from journals like Journal of Organizational Behavior or PLoS ONE) — Synthesizes multiple empirical findings to assess consistency and effect size, addressing the disputed status and moderate confidence level.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental study comparing self-reported productivity in remote vs. on-site work with objective productivity metrics (e.g., using time-tracking or output data from a technology firm) — Helps disentangle subjective perception from actual performance, testing whether the decrease is a perceptual bias or reflects genuine productivity loss.

C006.subject: Remote work
C006.object: objective output per hour only when task interdependence is high
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work objective output per hour only when task interdependence is high]

[PATH:empirical] Meta-analysis of field experiments comparing remote vs. on-site productivity across teams with varying task interdependence (e.g., Bloom et al., 2015; Choudhury et al., 2021) — Directly tests the interaction between remote work and task interdependence on objective output per hour, using controlled variation in interdependence.

[PATH:empirical] Laboratory or quasi-experimental study manipulating task interdependence (low vs. high) and work mode (remote vs. co-located) while measuring individual throughput on standardized tasks — Isolates the causal effect of interdependence on remote productivity, ruling out confounding factors like team composition or task type.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of coordination costs and communication delays in remote settings, predicting that high interdependence amplifies productivity losses (e.g., based on organizational economics or team cognition literature) — Provides mechanistic grounding for the hypothesis, identifying testable predictions about communication frequency, task switching, and output quality.

qualifier.condition: in roles requiring frequent synchronous collaboration

C007.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work objective output per hour]

[PATH:empirical] Bloom, N., et al. (2021). 'Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment.' Quarterly Journal of Economics. — This randomized controlled trial provides direct causal evidence on remote work productivity, including objective output per hour, which can be compared to the pandemic context.

[PATH:empirical] Gibbs, M., Mengel, F., & Siemroth, C. (2021). 'Work from Home & Productivity: Evidence from a Software Firm.' IZA Discussion Paper. — This study uses high-frequency productivity data from a global software firm during COVID-19, allowing direct measurement of output per hour changes under remote work.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of remote work productivity studies (e.g., Gajendran & Harrison, 2007, updated with pandemic-era data). — A systematic review and meta-analysis can aggregate effect sizes across multiple contexts, clarifying whether the increase holds generally or depends on specific conditions.

qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on developed economies
